Rajasthan Oxytocin Quality Investigation

After five women died following childbirth at two Kota hospitals, Rajasthan banned a TOCIN oxytocin injection whose sample failed quality testing, and later cancelled a Kota distributor’s licence. State and AIIMS investigations reported by The Indian Express did not attribute the deaths to the ineffective drug, and described gaps in clinical monitoring and documentation.

Causality not established. The investigations reported in the sources did not show that this product caused the deaths or harm described. Treat every link below as unproven unless a source says otherwise.

RETROSPECTIVE ILLUSTRATION

How Vyom Could Support This Investigation

Vyom could help investigators assemble product identity, batch, distribution, storage, administration, clinical and regulatory records into one connected evidence trail.

Written after the fact to illustrate potential capabilities. Vyom did not detect, investigate or prevent this incident, and holds none of its records.

SUGGESTED QUESTIONS

Verified facts

No official document has been read for this record, so “verified” here means corroborated by independent outlets.

  • Five women died after childbirth by caesarean section at hospitals in Kota.

    CORROBORATED[1][3]

  • TOCIN oxytocin injection failed laboratory testing for its oxytocin content.

    CORROBORATED[1][2]

  • Rajasthan’s Drug Control Department took regulatory action against the TOCIN supply chain.

    CORROBORATED[1][2]

Reported claims

Reported by one outlet and not independently confirmed.

  • Rajasthan’s Drug Control Department banned the sale and use of TOCIN (Oxytocin Injection 5 ml) after a sample failed quality tests.

    SINGLE REPORT[1]

  • The Drug Controller said the 5 ml sample passed bacterial endotoxin and sterility tests but did not contain the required quantity of oxytocin.

    “the required quantity of oxytocin was not found in the injection”
    SINGLE REPORT[1]

  • Around 3,500 vials were seized from Kota government hospital and other stockists linked to the supply chain.

    SINGLE REPORT[1]

  • Officials said the banned 5 ml injection belonged to a different batch from the 1 ml injections of the same company that the Kota medical college procured locally.

    SINGLE REPORT[1]

  • The Rajasthan Drug Testing Laboratory in Jaipur declared a batch of Tocin 1 ml spurious after tests found no trace of oxytocin.

    “contained no trace of oxytocin, its active ingredient”
    SINGLE REPORT[2][3]

  • A Kota distributor was alleged to have bought 9,300 units of Tocin 1 ml but sold 10,050 from the same batch; its wholesale and Schedule X licences were cancelled.

    SINGLE REPORT[2]

  • Regulators from three states, along with the apex drug controller, were reported to have acted against the manufacturer and distributor. The states are not named.

    SINGLE REPORT[3]

  • Investigators found the five women died of different medical conditions, with no single common cause.

    SINGLE REPORT[3]

  • Investigators reported missing records of hourly blood pressure and pulse, urine output, liver function tests and medication administration, and no autopsy in two cases.

    SINGLE REPORT[3]

  • Earlier, the Drug Controller said the banned injections had no direct link with the deaths, as the women had caesarean deliveries.

    SINGLE REPORT[1]

Unknown or not established

The sources say this is unknown or was not shown.

  • The Rajasthan expert committee did not attribute the deaths to the missing oxytocin.

    “the absence of active pharmaceutical ingredient oxytocin cannot be attributed to mortality”
    NOT ESTABLISHED[3]

Clinical chronology

WHAT RECORDS EXIST

No administration records, dosing times or patient-level timelines are public. Only the aggregate findings below were reported, from unreleased investigation reports.

  • Two deaths were recorded at JK Lone Hospital: one attributed to pre-existing heart disease, one to complications of postpartum haemorrhage.

    SINGLE REPORT[3]

  • Three deaths were recorded at New Medical College Hospital, attributed to disseminated intravascular coagulation, hypovolemic shock and stitch chorioamnionitis.

    SINGLE REPORT[3]

  • The committee noted that clinical records did not mention additional oxytocic or uterotonic medicines in any case.

    “in no case there has been any mention of having been given additional oxytocic or uterotonic medications as per clinical records”
    SINGLE REPORT[3]

  • Autopsies were not conducted in two cases where they could have established the cause of death.

    SINGLE REPORT[3]

Evidence gaps

  • No batch or lot numbers appear in any source read.
  • Whether the 1 ml injections used at the Kota hospitals came from the batch declared spurious is not stated.
  • The three states whose regulators acted are not named.
  • The ban order, licence-cancellation order and laboratory reports have not been read directly — only as reported.
  • The committee reports are unreleased; their findings are known only as reported by The Indian Express.
  • Distribution beyond Kota stockists is not documented in the sources read.

Suggested review steps

SUGGESTED · FOR A QUALIFIED REVIEWER
  1. 01Obtain the ban order and the laboratory report for the 5 ml sample, including its batch number.
  2. 02Obtain the laboratory report that declared the 1 ml batch spurious, including its batch number.
  3. 03Compare both batch numbers with the Kota hospitals’ pharmacy issue records.
  4. 04Request the distributor’s purchase and sale invoices and the manufacturer’s dispatch letter, and reconcile the 750-unit difference.
  5. 05Through authorised access only, review medication administration records for the 12 patients the committee examined.
  6. 06Confirm with regulators which three states acted, and on which products and batches.
  7. 07Record each conclusion with its evidence, the reviewer and the reason.

Suggestions only. A qualified reviewer decides what to do, and records why.
